\chapter{The Past That Takes être}
\label{ch:passe-compose-etre}
\hlchaptermodality{20}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can choose between avoir and être in the past, and say what the participle agrees with and why.}

A short closed list of verbs refuses avoir and takes être, and it is easier as a shape than a list: arriving and leaving, in space or in life. Two corrections come with it — motion verbs like courir take avoir, because motion is not transition, and five verbs switch to avoir the moment they take an object, which shows the rule is about the sentence rather than the verb. Then the agreement, which is audible for once: elle est morte. And underneath avoir's rule, être's rule and the pronominal rule sits one fact — the participle was an adjective, and it agrees with whatever it described.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[je suis allé]{je suis allé — the past built from \textquotedblleft{}be\textquotedblright{}}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-suis-alle}



\begin{quote}
You built a past tense out of \emph{avoir}. Now meet the verbs that will not have it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: some verbs take être instead}]
The recipe is the same shape as before, with the other verb in front:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{être} (conjugated) \textbf{+ past participle}
\end{quote}

\textbf{aller}, \textquotedblleft{}to go,\textquotedblright{} is the headline case. Its past is \textbf{not} \emph{j'ai allé}. It is:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{je suis allé} — I went
  \item \textbf{tu es allé} — you went
  \item \textbf{il est allé} — he went
  \item \textbf{nous sommes allés} — we went
  \item \textbf{ils sont allés} — they went
\end{itemize}

Say \emph{j'ai allé} to a French speaker and it will land as clearly wrong, the way \emph{I have went} lands in English.

So you now have two past tenses that are really one tense with two auxiliaries, and the only question a verb ever raises is: \textbf{which one?} For the vast majority it is \emph{avoir}, and this chapter is about the short list that says otherwise — what is on it, what is deceptively not on it, and the visible thing that happens to the participle when \emph{être} is used.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}je suis allé, tu es allé, il est allé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé … je suis allé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the error, so you can hear it — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai allé is wrong, like \emph{I have went}\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé … je suis allé\textquotedblright{}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you say \textquotedblleft{}I went\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Je suis allé}.) Which auxiliary does \emph{aller} take? (\emph{\textbf{être}}.) What is wrong with \emph{j'ai allé}? (\textbf{The wrong auxiliary} — it sounds like \emph{I have went}.) Which auxiliary do most French verbs take? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}}.) Next: which verbs are on the short list.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[aller · venir · naître · mourir]{aller · venir · naître · mourir — the shape of the list}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-famille-etre}



\begin{quote}
Textbooks give this as a list to memorise, usually a dozen verbs long. It is much easier to hold as a shape.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: arriving and leaving}]
The verbs that take \emph{être} are these: \emph{aller} (go), \emph{venir} (come), \emph{partir} (leave), \emph{arriver} (arrive), \emph{entrer}, \emph{sortir}, \emph{monter}, \emph{descendre}, \emph{naître} (be born), \emph{mourir} (die), \emph{rester} (stay), \emph{tomber} (fall).

Read them as a \textbf{shape} and the list stops needing memorising:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{going, coming, being born, dying} — arriving and leaving, in space or in life.
\end{quote}

Every one of them is about \textbf{crossing a threshold}. Entering or leaving a place; entering or leaving the world; going up, going down, falling, staying put at the end of a movement. They are not verbs about \textbf{doing} something. They are verbs about \textbf{ending up somewhere}.

Hold on to that phrasing, because it is what makes the next two lessons make sense. It is also why the participle behaves the way it does: if the verb describes where you \textbf{ended up}, the participle is describing \textbf{you} — and you will see it agree with you accordingly.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four corners — \textquotedblleft{}going, coming, born, dying\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shape — \textquotedblleft{}arriving and leaving, in space or in life\textquotedblright{}
  \item the test — \textquotedblleft{}not doing something; ending up somewhere\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}je suis allé, je suis venu, je suis resté\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the shape of the \emph{être} list in one line. (\textbf{Arriving and leaving, in space or in life} — going, coming, being born, dying.) What do all these verbs have in common? (They cross a \textbf{threshold} — they are about \textbf{ending up somewhere}, not about doing something.) Name three. (\emph{aller}, \emph{venir}, \emph{partir}, \emph{naître}, \emph{mourir}, \emph{rester}, \emph{tomber} — any three.) Next: the verbs that look like they belong and do not.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[j'ai couru]{j'ai couru — not every motion verb qualifies}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-pas-tout-mouvement}



\begin{quote}
\textquotedblleft{}Verbs of motion take \emph{être}\textquotedblright{} is the rule most learners are given, and it will mislead you within a week.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: moving is not arriving}]
These are all motion verbs, and every one of them takes \textbf{avoir}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{marcher} (walk) — \emph{j'ai marché}
  \item \textbf{courir} (run) — \emph{j'ai couru}
  \item \textbf{nager} (swim), \textbf{danser} (dance), \textbf{voyager} (travel)
\end{itemize}

You can run for an hour and arrive nowhere. That is the whole distinction. The \emph{être} verbs are not about \textbf{movement}; they are about \textbf{arriving, leaving and changing state} — crossing a threshold, as the last lesson put it.

\emph{Courir} describes what your legs did. \emph{Partir} describes that you are no longer here. The first is an activity; the second is a change in where you are, and it is the change that takes \emph{être}.

So correct the rule in your head now, before it costs you anything: \textbf{not motion — transition.}
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the avoir ones — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai marché, j'ai couru, j'ai dansé\textquotedblright{}
  \item against the être ones — \textquotedblleft{}je suis parti, je suis arrivé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the corrected rule — \textquotedblleft{}not motion, transition\textquotedblright{}
  \item the test — \textquotedblleft{}you can run for an hour and arrive nowhere\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which auxiliary does \emph{courir} take? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}} — \emph{j'ai couru}.) But is it not a motion verb? (\textbf{Yes} — which is why \textquotedblleft{}motion verbs take \emph{être}\textquotedblright{} is the \textbf{wrong rule}.) State the right one. (\textbf{Transition, not motion} — arriving, leaving, changing state.) Next: the verbs that use both.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[je suis monté / j'ai monté les valises]{je suis monté / j'ai monté les valises}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-bascule}



\begin{quote}
A handful of verbs sit on both sides of the line, and which side they are on depends on the sentence rather than the verb.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: an object flips the auxiliary}]
\textbf{monter}, \textbf{descendre}, \textbf{sortir}, \textbf{rentrer} and \textbf{passer} take \emph{être} when they stand alone, and \emph{avoir} the moment they take a \textbf{direct object}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Je suis monté.} — \textquotedblleft{}I went up.\textquotedblright{} No object; \emph{être}.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{J'ai monté les valises.} — \textquotedblleft{}I took the suitcases up.\textquotedblright{} An object; \emph{avoir}.
\end{quote}

This looks like an extra rule to memorise. It is the opposite: it is the rule you already have, doing exactly what it said it would.

\emph{Je suis monté} describes \textbf{where I ended up} — a transition, so \emph{être}. \emph{J'ai monté les valises} describes \textbf{something I did to the suitcases} — an action on an object, so \emph{avoir}. The verb has not changed its meaning much; what has changed is whether the sentence is about a transition or about an action, and that is the only thing the auxiliary has ever cared about.

So these verbs are not exceptions. They are the clearest demonstration that the rule is about the \textbf{sentence}, not the verb.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the pair — \textquotedblleft{}Je suis monté … J'ai monté les valises\textquotedblright{}
  \item the same for going out — \textquotedblleft{}Je suis sorti … J'ai sorti le chien\textquotedblright{}
  \item the reason — \textquotedblleft{}transition takes être; an action on an object takes avoir\textquotedblright{}
  \item the conclusion — \textquotedblleft{}what decides it is the sentence, not the verb\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which auxiliary in \emph{je suis monté}? (\emph{\textbf{être}} — no object, a transition.) And in \emph{j'ai monté les valises}? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}} — a \textbf{direct object}.) Is this a new rule? (\textbf{No} — it is the same rule: transition takes \emph{être}, an action on an object takes \emph{avoir}.) Next: what happens to the participle.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[elle est allée]{elle est allée — the participle agrees}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-accord-sujet}



\begin{quote}
With \emph{avoir}, the participle almost never moved. With \emph{être} it moves every time, and this is the one agreement in French you can actually hear.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: it agrees with the subject}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{French} & \textbf{English} \\
\midrule
Il est \textbf{allé}. & He went. \\
Elle est \textbf{allée}. & She went. \\
Ils sont \textbf{allés}. & They went. \\
Elles sont \textbf{allées}. & They (f.) went. \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The participle takes the \textbf{subject's} gender and number — exactly like an adjective.

And the reason is the same fossil you already met. \emph{Elle est allée} began as a plain description: \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{she is gone},\textquotedblright{} with \emph{gone} describing \textbf{her}, in the same way \emph{elle est fatiguée} describes her. It was never an action she performed on something. It was a \textbf{state she was in} — which is precisely the shape of every verb on this list. So the participle agreed with her, and it still does.

One practical note. With \emph{aller} you cannot hear the difference: \emph{allé} and \emph{allée} are identical aloud. But some of these verbs end in a consonant, and then you can — \emph{il est mort} against \emph{elle est morte}, where the \textbf{t} wakes up. That makes this the rare French agreement rule that is not purely a spelling problem.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four — \textquotedblleft{}il est allé, elle est allée, ils sont allés, elles sont allées\textquotedblright{}
  \item one you can hear — \textquotedblleft{}il est mort, elle est morte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the reason — \textquotedblleft{}she is gone: gone describes her\textquotedblright{}
  \item the parallel — \textquotedblleft{}elle est fatiguée, elle est allée\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
With \emph{être}, what does the participle agree with? (The \textbf{subject}.) Say \textquotedblleft{}she went.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Elle est allée}.) Why does it agree? (It began as a \textbf{description of her} — \textquotedblleft{}she is gone\textquotedblright{} — so it behaved like an \textbf{adjective}.) Which example lets you \textbf{hear} the agreement? (\emph{\textbf{il est mort}} against \emph{\textbf{elle est morte}}.) Next: the one rule under both auxiliaries.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[une seule règle]{une seule règle — both halves are the same fact}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-accord-unifie}



\begin{quote}
You now have two agreement rules that look unrelated. They are one rule, and seeing that is worth more than either of them.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the participle agrees with whatever it described}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{auxiliary} & \textbf{the participle agrees with} & \textbf{because it was…} \\
\midrule
\emph{avoir} & a \textbf{preceding object} — \emph{les lettres que j'ai écrites} & \textquotedblleft{}I have letters, \textbf{written}\textquotedblright{} \\
\emph{être} & the \textbf{subject} — \emph{elle est allée} & \textquotedblleft{}she is \textbf{gone}\textquotedblright{} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Two rules, two different targets — and one explanation covering both.

The participle \textbf{was an adjective}, and an adjective agrees with the thing it describes. That is all either rule says.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item With \emph{avoir}, the thing described was the \textbf{object you possessed}: the letters are the written ones. So the participle agrees with the object — and only when the object comes first, because that is where an adjective could still reach it.
  \item With \emph{être}, the thing described was the \textbf{subject}: she is the gone one. So the participle agrees with her.
\end{itemize}

Both are the same sentence-shape from Latin, one built on \emph{habēre} and one built on \emph{esse}, and in both the participle is doing an adjective's job.

French textbooks teach these as two chapters and a long list of exceptions. They are one idea with a two-thousand-year memory, and once you have the idea most of those exceptions write themselves.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the avoir case — \textquotedblleft{}les lettres que j'ai écrites\textquotedblright{}
  \item the être case — \textquotedblleft{}elle est allée\textquotedblright{}
  \item the single rule — \textquotedblleft{}the participle agrees with whatever it described\textquotedblright{}
  \item the two old sentences — \textquotedblleft{}I have letters written … she is gone\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
With \emph{avoir}, what does the participle agree with? (A \textbf{preceding object}.) With \emph{être}? (The \textbf{subject}.) State the one rule underneath both. (The participle \textbf{was an adjective} and agrees with \textbf{whatever it described}.) Why does the \emph{avoir} rule need the object to come first? (Because that is where an \textbf{adjective could still reach it}.) Next: the verbs that take \emph{être} and ignore its rule.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[je me suis levé]{je me suis levé — the pronominal family}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-pronominal-etre}



\begin{quote}
The \emph{être} list was short and closed. Here is one more family that takes \emph{être}, and it has no end to it.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: all of them, without exception}]
A \textbf{pronominal} verb is one carrying the little reflexive pronoun you met when you learned to give your name — the \emph{me} of \emph{je m'appelle}, the \emph{se} of \emph{s'appeler}.

\textbf{Every one of them takes \emph{être} in the past.} No list, no shape to memorise, no exceptions:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{je me suis levé} — I got up
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{elle s'est lavée} — she washed
\end{quote}

Notice the word order: the reflexive pronoun comes \textbf{before} the auxiliary, not after it. \emph{Je \textbf{me} suis levé}, not \emph{je suis me levé}.

That gives you two ways into \emph{être}, and they work differently. The verbs from the earlier list are a \textbf{closed set} you can hold as a shape. The pronominals are an \textbf{open class} identified by their form — if it has a \emph{me}, \emph{te} or \emph{se}, it takes \emph{être}, and you never have to ask.

But be careful with what comes next. They take \emph{être}, and they do \textbf{not} follow \emph{être}'s agreement rule.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}je me suis levé\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}elle s'est lavée\textquotedblright{}
  \item the word order — \textquotedblleft{}je \emph{me} suis levé\textquotedblright{}; the pronoun comes first
  \item the rule — \textquotedblleft{}if it has me, te or se, it takes être\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which auxiliary do pronominal verbs take? (\emph{\textbf{être}} — \textbf{all} of them.) How do you recognise one? (It carries \textbf{me, te} or \textbf{se}.) Where does that pronoun sit? (\textbf{Before the auxiliary} — \emph{je me suis levé}.) Is this a closed list like the earlier one? (\textbf{No} — it is an \textbf{open class}.) Next: the trap in their agreement.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[elle s'est lavée / elle s'est lavé les …]{elle s'est lavée — the auxiliary lies about the rule}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-pronominal-accord}



\begin{quote}
Pronominal verbs take \emph{être}. Now watch them ignore \emph{être}'s agreement rule completely.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: être on the outside, avoir underneath}]
They agree with a \textbf{preceding direct object} — which is \emph{avoir}'s rule, not \emph{être}'s. Usually that object \textbf{is} the reflexive pronoun, and sometimes it is not:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Elle s'est lavée.} — She washed \textbf{herself}. \emph{se} is the direct object, and it comes first, so the participle agrees.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Elle s'est lavé les mains.} — She washed \textbf{her hands}. The object is \emph{les mains}, and it \textbf{follows}, so there is no agreement.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Elles se sont parlé.} — They spoke \textbf{to each other}. \emph{se} is \textbf{indirect} — you speak \emph{to} someone — so there is no agreement.
\end{quote}

Which is, satisfyingly, the rule you already had. Nothing new has been introduced: the participle agrees with a preceding \textbf{direct} object, exactly as it did in \emph{les lettres que j'ai écrites}.

The lesson to take is about \textbf{appearances}. The auxiliary looks like \emph{être} and the agreement behaves like \emph{avoir}, and if you let the first tell you about the second you will get it wrong every time. The auxiliary is not what decides agreement; it never was. What decides it is what the participle is describing.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item agreement — \textquotedblleft{}Elle s'est lavée\textquotedblright{}
  \item no agreement, object after — \textquotedblleft{}Elle s'est lavé les mains\textquotedblright{}
  \item no agreement, indirect — \textquotedblleft{}Elles se sont parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the warning — \textquotedblleft{}the auxiliary looks like être; the agreement is avoir's\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which agreement rule do pronominal verbs follow? (\emph{\textbf{avoir\emph{'s\textbf{ — a }preceding direct object\textbf{.) Why does \emph{elle s'est lavée} agree? (\emph{se} is the }direct object\textbf{ and comes }first\textbf{.) Why does \emph{elle s'est lavé les mains} not? (The object is \emph{les mains} and it }follows\textbf{.) Why does \emph{elles se sont parlé} not? (\emph{se} is }indirect\textbf{ — you speak \emph{to} someone.) Next: the group that escapes even this.}}}}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[elles se sont souvenues]{elles se sont souvenues — the verbs with no other form}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-pronominal-seul}



\begin{quote}
One small group escapes even the rule you just learned, and it escapes for a reason you can work out rather than memorise.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: no object to be an object of}]
A few verbs exist \textbf{only} in pronominal form. There is no plain version of them at all:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{se souvenir} — to remember
  \item \textbf{s'enfuir} — to flee
  \item \textbf{s'évanouir} — to faint
\end{itemize}

There is no \emph{souvenir quelqu'un}, no \emph{enfuir quelque chose}. The \emph{se} is not doing a job you could describe as direct or indirect, because there is no non-reflexive verb for it to be the object \textbf{of}. It is simply part of the word.

So the previous lesson's test cannot be run on them, and they fall back to agreeing with the \textbf{subject}:

\begin{quote}
\textbf{Elles se sont souvenues.} — They remembered.
\end{quote}

Which is where this chapter's whole argument lands. The agreement is not decided by the auxiliary, and not by a list of verb types. It is decided by \textbf{what the participle is describing} — and when there is no object in the picture at all, the only thing left for it to describe is the subject.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the three — \textquotedblleft{}se souvenir, s'enfuir, s'évanouir\textquotedblright{}
  \item the example — \textquotedblleft{}Elles se sont souvenues\textquotedblright{}
  \item the reason — \textquotedblleft{}no plain verb, so the \emph{se} is not an object of anything\textquotedblright{}
  \item the landing — \textquotedblleft{}what is left for the participle to describe is the subject\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What is special about \emph{se souvenir}? (It exists \textbf{only} in pronominal form — there is no plain \emph{souvenir} verb.) So what does its participle agree with? (The \textbf{subject} — \emph{elles se sont souvenues}.) Why can the direct-object test not be applied? (There is \textbf{no non-reflexive verb} for \emph{se} to be the object of.) Next: all of it together.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — which auxiliary, and what agrees}

\label{lesson:FR-C16-practice-etre-past}



\begin{quote}
Two questions cover this whole chapter: which auxiliary, and what does the participle describe. Run both.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Your turn: which auxiliary}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the contrast — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai parlé … je suis allé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the shape of the list — \textquotedblleft{}arriving and leaving, in space or in life\textquotedblright{}
  \item the trap — \textquotedblleft{}j'ai couru, j'ai marché\textquotedblright{}; motion is not transition
  \item the switch — \textquotedblleft{}je suis monté … j'ai monté les valises\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\emph{Twice through:} \textquotedblleft{}je suis allé, je suis venu, je suis resté\textquotedblright{}

\subsection*{Your turn: what the participle agrees with}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item the four — \textquotedblleft{}il est allé, elle est allée, ils sont allés, elles sont allées\textquotedblright{}
  \item the audible one — \textquotedblleft{}il est mort, elle est morte\textquotedblright{}
  \item the avoir side — \textquotedblleft{}les lettres que j'ai écrites\textquotedblright{}
  \item the single rule — \textquotedblleft{}it agrees with whatever it described\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\subsection*{Your turn: the pronominals}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}je me suis levé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the three cases — \textquotedblleft{}elle s'est lavée; elle s'est lavé les mains; elles se sont parlé\textquotedblright{}
  \item the group with no plain form — \textquotedblleft{}elles se sont souvenues\textquotedblright{}
\end{itemize}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built this chapter}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{a second auxiliary}, and a short closed list that is easier as a shape than a list: \textbf{arriving and leaving, in space or in life}.
  \item \textbf{two corrections to the rule you would have been given.} \emph{Motion} verbs do not take \emph{être} — \textbf{transition} verbs do; and five verbs switch the moment they take an object, which shows that what decides the auxiliary is the \textbf{sentence}, not the verb.
  \item \textbf{an agreement you can hear} — \emph{il est mort}, \emph{elle est morte}.
  \item \textbf{one rule under everything}: the participle was an adjective, and it agrees with whatever it described. \emph{Avoir}'s rule, \emph{être}'s rule and the pronominal rule are that one fact seen from three angles.
\end{itemize}
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Say \textquotedblleft{}she went.\textquotedblright{} (\textbf{Elle est allée}.) Which auxiliary does \emph{courir} take, and why? (\emph{\textbf{avoir}} — it is \textbf{motion}, not \textbf{transition}.) What flips \emph{monter} to \emph{avoir}? (A \textbf{direct object}.) Which agreement rule do pronominal verbs follow? (\emph{\textbf{avoir\emph{'s\textbf{ — a preceding }direct\textbf{ object.) State the one rule under all of it. (The participle }agrees with whatever it described\textbf{.)}}}}
\end{tcolorbox}
